clue.text: Old financier certain to have a place in the city

indicators.note: the word for certain is given a place inside the city, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: Ur is the ancient Mesopotamian city, a crossword staple
certain means sure

explanation.surface: An old banker is sure to find somewhere to live in the city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to have a place in' puts SURE inside UR, the ancient city of Abraham.
explanation.definitionFit: A moneylender charging extortionate interest, the classic figure of old-fashioned finance.

clue.text: Down Having organic disease caused by chewing pencils?

indicators.note: chewing mangles the pencils, so their letters are reworked into a new order

explanation.surface: A child who chews pencils might be warned that it will make them ill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'chewing' rearranges PENCILS. The leading 'Down' is the newspaper's column heading caught up in the clue text and plays no part.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective relates to the spleen, an organ, so a splenic condition is a disease of that organ.

clue.text: Ready to complain, having lost head

indicators.note: losing its head means the word for complain drops its first letter

parts.note: to gripe is to complain

explanation.surface: Someone is about to grumble after losing their temper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'having lost head' drops the G from GRIPE.
explanation.definitionFit: Fruit that is ripe is ready for eating, and a person ripe for something is prepared for it.

clue.text: Duplicated English exercise externally assessed

indicators.note: the word for assessed lies outside, wrapping the other pieces

parts.note: assessed means rated
PE is physical education, school exercise

explanation.surface: An English assignment marked twice by an outside examiner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'externally' puts RATED around E and PE: R(EPE)ATED.
explanation.definitionFit: Something duplicated has been done or produced again, a copy of the first.

clue.text: He'll usually have several layers around him

definitions.text: He'll usually have several layers around him

parts.words: He'll usually have several layers around him
parts.note: layers reads like clothing in thick layers, but the layers are egg-laying hens surrounding a male bird in the farmyard

explanation.surface: A man who always dresses in several layers of clothing.
explanation.walkthrough: Layers suggests clothing; here it means hens, which lay eggs, gathered round the cock of the yard.
explanation.definitionFit: The male chicken lives among the hens of a flock, which are egg layers.

clue.text: Spell disaster?

parts.note: spell is read as a wizard's work and disaster as an aircraft crash in old RAF slang, together a famous wartime phrase

explanation.surface: Something that would foretell a calamity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spell disaster' looks like 'foretell trouble'. In RAF slang of the Second World War, wizard meant excellent and a prang was a crash, so the phrase was a spectacular crash.
explanation.definitionFit: A magician casts spells and a prang is a crash, so a crash by a sorcerer fits, and the RAF phrase meant a spectacular smash.

clue.text: A dessert's sent back — it's on the cool side

indicators.note: a dish sent back in a restaurant is returned, so the word for the dessert is read backwards

parts.note: a fool is a fruit and cream dessert

explanation.surface: Someone sends a pudding back to the kitchen because it is too cold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sent back' turns FOOL into LOOF, after A. A fool is a British pudding of fruit folded into cream.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who is distant and reserved is cool in manner, standing apart from others.

clue.text: Extreme article on beer evokes outstanding support

parts.note: far means extreme, as in the far left
an article is a thing, an object
ale is beer

explanation.surface: A remote item on beer brings to mind a remarkable backing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outstanding' means sticking out: the hooped frame of Tudor dress made skirts stand out from the body.
explanation.definitionFit: A framework of hoops worn under a skirt in the sixteenth century, supporting it so it stood out widely.

clue.text: bends no matter what

clue.text: Chips, for instance, produced by a virtuoso?

definitions.meaning: Mr Chips is the retired schoolmaster of the novel Goodbye, Mr Chips, a teacher of former days
a virtuoso is an expert, a skilled hand at something

explanation.surface: Asks whether chips are something a great performer turns out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chips' looks like food; it is Mr Chips, the elderly schoolmaster of James Hilton's novel, so a master of the past.
explanation.definitionFit: Read as two words it is a former teacher like Mr Chips; as an idiom it means an expert, a virtuoso.

clue.text: Phone located by the fence?

definitions.meaning: the handset of a telephone is the part held to the ear
a fence in criminal slang is someone who handles stolen goods

explanation.surface: Asks whether a telephone was found beside the garden fence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fence' suggests a garden boundary; in criminal slang it is a dealer in stolen goods.
explanation.definitionFit: The handset of a telephone takes in calls, and a handler of stolen goods takes them in from thieves.

clue.text: Church in middle of island stands on these rocky, glacial features

indicators.note: in a down clue the first part stands on top of the next
the church sits in the middle of the island abbreviation, one piece within another

parts.note: CE is the Church of England

indicators.note: rocky means unsteady, so the letters of these are shaken into a new order

explanation.surface: A church in the middle of an island stands on rocky glacial ground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in middle of' puts CE inside IS; 'rocky' rearranges THESE into HEETS; 'stands on' places ICES above HEETS in the down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Vast layers of glacier ice covering land, like those over Antarctica, are glacial features.

clue.text: Light from church on hill

parts.note: a tor is a rocky hill, as on Dartmoor

explanation.surface: A light shines from a church on a hilltop.
explanation.walkthrough: A tor is a rocky hilltop, common in the moors of southwest England.
explanation.definitionFit: A hand-held lamp or flaming brand gives light.

clue.text: Requirement for photography exhibition put on by Enfield, maybe?

indicators.note: in a down clue the first piece is placed on top of the second

parts.note: a flash is a showy display, an exhibition
the Enfield is a rifle made at Enfield, an example of a gun

explanation.surface: A photography exhibition staged in the London suburb of Enfield.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Enfield' looks like the north London borough; it is the Lee-Enfield rifle, made there. 'put on by' places FLASH above GUN.
explanation.definitionFit: A device firing a burst of light so a photographer can shoot in the dark.

clue.text: Living quarters about to be provided for chaplain

parts.note: a pad is slang for a home, someone's living quarters
re means about, concerning

explanation.surface: Accommodation is going to be arranged for the chaplain.
explanation.definitionFit: A forces chaplain is called the padre, a title for a priest.

clue.text: Passing with no difficulty after a month?

indicators.note: the word for no difficulty comes after the month

parts.note: Dec is the abbreviation for December
ease means lack of difficulty

explanation.surface: Asks whether a test was passed easily after a month of study.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Passing' looks like succeeding in a test; it means dying.
explanation.definitionFit: Passing away is death, and the formal word for death is used in law.

clue.text: It makes you sick generally — no end to it

definitions.text: It makes you sick generally — no end to it

indicators.note: sick means disordered, so the remaining letters are jumbled
taking away the end means the last letter of generally is cut

explanation.surface: Something that gives you a general sickness that never stops.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no end to it' cuts the Y from GENERALLY, and 'sick' rearranges GENERALL. The whole clue also describes the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A substance such as pollen that triggers an immune reaction and makes sufferers ill.

clue.text: I'm embraced by girl with ugly face

indicators.note: embraced means held inside, so the girl's name wraps round the other piece

parts.note: Grace is a girl's name

explanation.surface: Someone is hugged by a girl with an unattractive face.
explanation.walkthrough: 'embraced by' puts IM inside GRACE: GR(IM)ACE.
explanation.definitionFit: A twisted expression of pain or disgust is an ugly face pulled on purpose.

clue.text: Race attack involves leading characters in loathsome organisation

indicators.note: involves means takes in, so the word for attack wraps round the other letters

parts.note: to slam is to attack in words, to criticise severely

indicators.note: the leading characters are the first letters of these two words

explanation.surface: A violent race attack carried out by a hateful group.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leading characters in' takes LO from loathsome organisation; 'involves' puts that inside SLAM: SLA(LO)M.
explanation.definitionFit: A downhill ski race weaving between gates.

clue.text: Problem involving an inordinate number of units?

definitions.text: Problem involving an inordinate number of units?

parts.words: Problem involving an inordinate number of units?
parts.note: units sounds like a maths question; here they are measures of drink, consumed to excess

explanation.surface: A maths problem involving a huge number of units.
explanation.walkthrough: 'units' suggests arithmetic; in Britain a unit is the standard measure of alcohol used in health advice.
explanation.definitionFit: Dependence on drink, measured in units consumed far beyond safe limits.

clue.text: Long-range weapon has South African endorsement

parts.note: the V1 was the German long-range flying bomb of the Second World War, written here as VI
SA is South Africa

explanation.surface: A long-range missile carries a South African stamp of approval.
explanation.walkthrough: The V1 flying bomb is written with the letters V and I in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: A stamp in a passport is an official endorsement permitting entry.

clue.text: Fizzy drink bottled in Hastings

indicators.note: bottled means held inside, so the answer is contained in the town's name

explanation.surface: A sparkling wine is bottled in the seaside town of Hastings.
explanation.walkthrough: Hastings is a seaside town in southeast England.
explanation.definitionFit: A sparkling Italian wine from Piedmont.

clue.text: For clearing -a collection of violin strings, about a pound

indicators.note: the strings go about the pound, wrapping round it
a collection gathers the strings together in any order, so their letters are rearranged

parts.note: a violin's four strings are tuned E, A, D and G
L is the abbreviation for a pound, from libra

explanation.surface: Asks what one uses to clear: a set of violin strings for about a pound.
explanation.walkthrough: 'collection of' rearranges EADG to GADE, and 'about' puts L inside: G(L)ADE.
explanation.definitionFit: An open space in a wood is a clearing.

clue.text: Make statutory provision after member is dead

parts.note: a leg is a limb, a member of the body
late means dead, as in the late king

explanation.surface: A law is passed after a member of parliament has died.
explanation.walkthrough: The page has 'ad'; the wordplay needs 'dead', which gives LATE.
explanation.definitionFit: To pass laws is to make provision by statute.

clue.text: Goods hastily disposed of, in the main

definitions.text: Goods hastily disposed of, in the main

parts.words: Goods hastily disposed of, in the main
parts.note: in the main reads as mostly, but it means at sea: cargo thrown overboard to lighten a ship

explanation.surface: Goods that, for the most part, were got rid of in a hurry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in the main' looks like 'mostly'; the main is the open sea.
explanation.definitionFit: Cargo thrown overboard to lighten a ship in distress, as opposed to wreckage floating free.

clue.text: Comeback for Jerusalem pressman is rumoured

indicators.note: a comeback is a return, so the name for Jerusalem is read backwards

parts.note: Sion is a variant of Zion, the hill and poetic name for Jerusalem
ED is an editor, a newspaper man

explanation.surface: A Jerusalem journalist returns, reportedly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Comeback for' turns SION into NOIS, then ED for editor.
explanation.definitionFit: News that has been spread around by talk has been made public.
